TextBlock.TextLine: Lloyd's Evening Post, Mon. May 6, - Wed. May 8, 1765, p.437
To the EDITOR of LLOYD'S EVENING POST.
THE superior excellence of the Artists'
Exhibition in Spring Garden, for this
year, is universally allowed, and the great re-
sort of spectators will appear by the large re-
ceipt of money, and I hope convince the Pre-
sident and Directors, that they cannot take too
much pains in dissiping such a collection be-
fore they open it. Many of the Paintings are
inimitable; and it is very evident, that the
Gladiator by Candle-light was done by a
young country Painter, ignorant of the arts
practised by the modern Masters, or, perhaps,
it had been Tullamoore'd, and passed off to
some supercilious Connoisseur, at a great price,
for an antique picture.
The two pieces done by the Premier Pein-
teur to Louis XV, throw a great lustre on the
Society of Artists of Great Britain; and must
serve to prove the French Masters are con-
vinced, that Excellency in the Polite Arts is not
confined to their Royal Academy or Louvre;
but, at present, is found in London, and car-
ried to as great a height as ever they were in
Paris. And to my countrymen, if there be
any that are infidels to this doctrine, I would
ask them, What reduced this year, the price
of the old Foreign Masters about 300l. per
cent lower than their prime cost, but the high
estimation of the present English Masters?
And in future time the works of a Barret,
Cotes, Gainsborough, Hayman, Marlow,
Meyer, Penny, Pine, Reynolds, Richards,
Sandby, Smart, Shaw, Wilson, the Wrights,
and Zaffanij will be equal in value to any of
the antient Masters; and if any of these were
only to signifiy their intentions of laying down
the pencil, their pictures would be immediate-
ly in greaten estimation and request; as was
the case of the ingenious Mr. Scot this season,
when some of his pictures were sold at Lang-
ford's, for a great deal more than ever he used
to paint them for when bespoke.
Among the engravers, &c. in comparison
with those of Paris, we equal in all the dif-
ferent branches, and excel them in most; as
for instance:
In Metzotinto, Mac Ardell, Fisher, and Wat-
son, have no competitors.
In Landscape, Woolet, Elliot, Sandby, and
Brown, excel.
In Historical, Strange, Walker, and Taylor,
are equal to most of the French.
And sorry I am to think, that the only re-
maining disciplie of Gravelot's School would
not oblige the Public with some of his per-
formances. What a great loss must the Polite
Arts have sustained, by having the greatest
Historical Engraving that ever England pro-
duced, buried, as it were, alive, for upwards
of twenty years (except in a Print of two
which he engraved after the Pictures of the
celebrated Hogarth,) by working only for the
London Booksellers?
Yours,
A Lover of the Arts.
